findings.checklist_item: - [ ] State exactly when the helper returns `untrusted` on a config error (e.g. only when REBAR_VERIFY_TRUSTED_OPCERT_KEYS or the TOML key is present but fails coercion), and what happens when config load fails for an unrelated key.
evidence: "If the list cannot be read or coerced, the helper fails closed (`untrusted`, reason names the config error), never \"unset\"."
"List unset: unchanged in this story."
"requires ... decodable base64, else `ConfigError` naming the entry position"
findings.finding: The fail-closed rule is ambiguous about scope. Step 1 says a malformed entry raises `ConfigError` at coercion, which normally aborts config load. Step 2 then says that when 'the list cannot be read or coerced' the helper returns `untrusted` and treats this as 'never unset'. The plan does not say how the helper tells a malformed trust list apart from an unrelated config error, or from a list that is genuinely unset. If any config error forces `untrusted`, the list-unset path is no longer 'unchanged' (AC2).
findings.location: Approach step 2 (fail closed) vs step 1 (ConfigError) and AC2
scenarios: A malformed unrelated key, e.g. verify.plan_review_engine, causes config load to raise; the helper cannot tell whether the trust list was set, so it either flips pin-file users to `untrusted` or silently falls back to pin-file trust.
findings.suggested_fix: Define the rule as follows: if the raw trust-list value is present (env var or TOML key) but `_as_trusted_key_list` raises, return `untrusted` naming the error. If the raw value is absent, use the list-unset path. Other config errors propagate as they do today.

findings.checklist_item: - [ ] In Approach step 2, say how the helper decides the list is 'set but unreadable' when `compose_config` raises (for example, check the raw TOML or env source for the `verify.trusted_opcert_keys` key before coercing it). Fail closed only in that case, keep unrelated config faults on the list-unset path, and add a test for each case.
evidence: src/rebar/_opcert_verify.py:78-87: `_required_environment` docstring says 'Unreadable config cannot enable a restriction', and `except Exception: return None` treats any config failure as unset
src/rebar/_config_sections.py:290-294: coercers run inside the whole-config load loop, so a `ConfigError` from one key aborts the composed config for all keys
Plan step 1: `_as_trusted_key_list` raises `ConfigError` on a malformed entry, and that error surfaces through `compose_config`, not through a list-scoped reader
Testing section: 'malformed list never `certified`' and 'List unset: pinned-key certificate verifies as before' both depend on this distinction, but the plan never says how it is made
findings.finding: Approach step 2 assumes the trust-list helper can tell a list that 'cannot be read or coerced' (fail closed → `untrusted`) apart from one that is unset (behaviour unchanged). The config layer gives it no way to do that. A malformed entry makes the coercer raise `ConfigError`, which aborts the whole `compose_config`. Any unrelated bad key does the same. Reading `config.compose_config(...).verify.trusted_opcert_keys` therefore yields either a value or an exception about the whole config, never a list-specific error. Failing closed on that exception would turn every op-cert `untrusted` even in repos that never set the list, which contradicts 'List unset: unchanged in this story'. Treating the exception as unset would mean a malformed list silently fails open. The plan's only precedent goes the other way: `_required_environment` swallows every config exception as 'no restriction'.
findings.location: Approach step 2 ('If the list cannot be read or coerced, the helper fails closed (`untrusted`, reason names the config error), never "unset"') vs 'List unset: unchanged in this story'
scenarios: A developer clone with no trust list but a typo in an unrelated `[verify]` key: compose_config raises, the helper fails closed, and every op-cert there flips from certified to `untrusted`. That breaks the 'unchanged when unset' AC and the plan-review claim gate.

The helper copies the `_required_environment` pattern (`except Exception: return None`): a malformed `REBAR_VERIFY_TRUSTED_OPCERT_KEYS` in the MCP container is read as unset, and the server quietly drops back to the pin-file path, failing open.
findings.suggested_fix: Make the helper check for the key before it coerces: if `REBAR_VERIFY_TRUSTED_OPCERT_KEYS` is in the environment, or the raw `[verify]` table has `trusted_opcert_keys`, treat the list as set. Then any `ConfigError` from composing config gives `untrusted` with the error text. If the key is absent from every source, keep the current path. Add a unit test showing that an unrelated malformed key with no list still certifies as before.

findings.checklist_item: - [ ] Say how the trust-list helper tells 'unset' from 'unreadable': which compose_config / ConfigError outcomes count as fail-closed `untrusted` and which as unset, and add a test for each case.
evidence: Plan: 'If the list cannot be read or coerced, the helper fails closed (`untrusted`, reason names the config error), never "unset". List unset: unchanged in this story.'
src/rebar/_opcert_verify.py:84-87 _required_environment wraps compose_config(...).verify.require_environment in `except Exception: return None` — compose faults today read as 'not configured'.
_config_sections.py: coercers raise ConfigError per key, and the whole compose fails, so a fault in another key looks the same as a fault in this one.
findings.finding: The plan says the helper fails closed ('untrusted') when the list 'cannot be read or coerced, never "unset"', and also that with the list unset nothing changes. It doesn't say how the helper tells 'unset' apart from 'unreadable'. Config is read via config.compose_config, which raises ConfigError on any bad key in the composed config (the existing _required_environment catches every exception and returns None). If the helper treats any compose failure as fail-closed, then deployments with no list but a config fault elsewhere start getting `untrusted` on every op-cert, which breaks the 'list unset: unchanged' AC. If it treats a compose failure as unset, a malformed list fails open.
findings.location: Approach step 2 ('If the list cannot be read or coerced, the helper fails closed …'); AC 2
scenarios: A library or CLI user with no list and a malformed unrelated key calls verify_signature. Under a fail-closed reading every op-cert becomes `untrusted`, a regression the plan says won't happen.

The MCP container has a malformed REBAR_VERIFY_TRUSTED_OPCERT_KEYS. If the implementer copies the _required_environment pattern, the error is swallowed as 'unset' and verification falls back to the pin file or embedded key, failing open.
findings.suggested_fix: Fail closed only when the fault is in verify.trusted_opcert_keys itself: the REBAR_VERIFY_TRUSTED_OPCERT_KEYS env var or the TOML key is present but fails _as_trusted_key_list, or the ConfigError names `verify.trusted_opcert_keys`. When compose fails on an unrelated key and the list source is absent, treat the list as unset (today's behaviour). Add tests for both cases to tests/unit/test_opcert_trust_list.py.

The plan names neither that helper nor a single shared membership function. Verification and `/health` could therefore each implement their own split-and-compare, and disagree on whether a key is listed (e.g. on whitespace or comment handling). findings.checklist_item: - [ ] State in Approach step 1 that the entry format is a deliberate subset of OpenSSH allowed_signers (principal = env_id; no options, no multi-principal lists). Justify the drop of the options field (valid-after/valid-before) and the Python membership check over the existing `allowed_signers_from_keys` + `ssh-keygen -Y verify` path, and say how the follow-on validity story will extend the format.
evidence: Plan: "requires `<env_id> <key-type> <base64> [comment]` with decodable base64"; "trust root is the SSHSIG's embedded key ... (principal, key type + body, comment ignored) not listed: new verdict `untrusted`"
src/rebar/attest/sshsig.py:36-37: "OpenSSH 8.9 is the floor: it introduced valid-after/valid-before validity intervals in allowed_signers, which the trust model relies on."
src/rebar/_opcert_verify.py:158 and :267 already render trusted keys with `authorship.allowed_signers_from_keys(keys, principal)` and verify through ssh-keygen.

Retrieved: pkg.go.dev/github.com/tionis/ssh-tools/allowed_signers ('The allowed_signers format is documented in the ssh-keygen(1) manual page'); github.com/jelmer/dulwich/discussions/1449 (naming and restricting a 'minimal sub-format of ssh-keygen allowed signers'); docs.gitlab.com SSH signed commits (allowed_signers maps identities to keys).
findings.finding: The trust-list entry grammar `<env_id> <key-type> <base64> [comment]` is a cut-down version of OpenSSH's allowed_signers line format (`principals [options] keytype base64 [comment]`), which the repo already uses as its trust-root format. The plan does not say it is a deliberate subset of that format. It also doesn't explain why it drops the options field (valid-after/valid-before), or why it adds a Python membership check instead of feeding the listed keys through the existing `allowed_signers_from_keys` + `ssh-keygen -Y verify` path.
findings.location: Approach step 1 (`_as_trusted_key_list` grammar) and step 2 (embedded-key trust root plus membership check)
scenarios: The follow-on story needs per-key validity or expiry. The list format has no options field, so the grammar has to be redesigned or a second parser added, instead of using allowed_signers' native valid-after/valid-before.

An operator writes an entry the allowed_signers way, e.g. `envA,envB ssh-ed25519 AAAA…` or with `namespaces="…"`. The comma-separated `REBAR_VERIFY_TRUSTED_OPCERT_KEYS` split breaks it into fragments and they get a ConfigError, with no documentation explaining that the syntax differs from allowed_signers.

src/rebar/config.py load_config docstring: "Resolve typed config: defaults < user < project < env < CLI". _config_probe_paths walks `rebar.toml` / `pyproject.toml` up to the git root.

Epic 0dd0-cecb-3932-4c90 operator decision: "Trust lives in that environment's own configuration, not in the repository."

Mitigation already in place: merge_sparse (_config_sections.py:301) replaces values per key, so the env value in the MCP container wins and the deployed server is unaffected. The risk is to environments with no env-layer list (review-bot, developer clones) and to future `require_environment` use. That is why this is advisory.
findings.finding: `verify.trusted_opcert_keys` is honoured from every config layer, including the project layer (`rebar.toml` / `pyproject.toml [tool.rebar]` committed to the repository). Any environment without an env or user override would then take an op-cert trust root from the repository. This brings back the repo-pinned trust that the epic is removing, and lets a change author add their own key and get a `trust_list` certification.
findings.location: Approach step 1 (config key / coercer in `_SECTIONS["verify"]`) and step 2 (`verify_opcert_record` trust check)
scenarios: A contributor's change adds `[tool.rebar.verify] trusted_opcert_keys = ["<their env> ssh-ed25519 <their key>"]` to pyproject.toml. The review-bot or a developer checkout of that change then reports the contributor's own op-certs as `certified` with trust basis `trust_list`, a label that implies operator-curated trust.

An operator later sets `verify.require_environment` on a host that has no env-layer list. A list committed to the repo then satisfies the requirement, which is self-certification through the repository.
findings.suggested_fix: In step 1, make `verify.trusted_opcert_keys` settable only from the user, env and CLI layers.
